For the scientific community no. It will make very little difference. 

The issue is that most folks don't have their ear to the ground when it comes to scientific research. The biggest impact I can see (as a researcher) is that when you publish something often times your institution will release a small press briefing upon request, these briefings will be the ones that the media picks up and writes about. 

Almost always if your research is interesting you will receive a call from a reporter who know nothing about your field and is only partially able to understand your work and its implications. They will ask you follow up questions and then have you explain things in terms that they understand. If you put up a barrier between the researcher and the journalist you are effectively ensuring that your findings will be misconstrued, misunderstood, or misappropriated by a group with an agenda. If you stop those press briefings from being published you can be sure that no one in the public will ever know anything about your work. Hell, even when you do explain it to reporters you often read the pop press article and marvel that it is only 90% correct.
